lesson.title: The First Shots: Fort Sumter and the Start of the Civil War
lesson.summary: The Confederate bombardment of Fort Sumter in Charleston Harbor on April 12 and 13, 1861, forced the fort's small Union garrison to surrender and turned the secession crisis into open war.
lesson.body:
By the time Lincoln took office on March 4, 1861, Fort Sumter had already become the most visible symbol of the standoff between the United States government and the newly formed Confederacy. The fort sat on an artificial island in Charleston Harbor, South Carolina, the very state that had led the secession movement, and its small Union garrison, roughly eighty soldiers under Major Robert Anderson, had occupied it since December 1860 after abandoning a less defensible position nearby. South Carolina and then the Confederate government demanded the fort's surrender, arguing that federal troops had no right to occupy Confederate territory, but Anderson refused to leave without orders, and the garrison's food supply was steadily running out.

Lincoln faced a genuine dilemma. Reinforcing the fort with troops risked being seen as an act of war, but abandoning it risked being seen as tacit recognition that secession was legitimate and that the Confederacy could simply seize federal property. Lincoln chose a middle path, notifying South Carolina's governor that he intended only to resupply the garrison with food, not additional soldiers or weapons, and leaving the decision to fire the first shot squarely with the Confederacy. Confederate President Jefferson Davis and his cabinet, under pressure from South Carolina officials who wanted the fort taken before the resupply ships could arrive, ordered General P.G.T. Beauregard to demand Anderson's surrender, and when Anderson refused, Confederate batteries surrounding the harbor opened fire before dawn on April 12, 1861.

The bombardment lasted roughly thirty four hours. Confederate guns fired thousands of rounds into the fort, setting fires and battering its walls, while Anderson's garrison returned fire with far less ammunition and no real hope of holding out. Remarkably, no one on either side was killed during the actual battle. Anderson surrendered on April 13, and the garrison was allowed to evacuate the next day under an agreement that included a ceremonial salute to the American flag; during that salute, an accidental explosion killed Private Daniel Hough, making him arguably the war's first fatality, ironically after the fighting itself had ended.

News of the attack transformed Northern public opinion almost overnight. Lincoln responded on April 15, 1861, by calling for 75,000 state militia volunteers to suppress what he described as a rebellion, a request that forced Virginia, Arkansas, Tennessee, and North Carolina to make their own choice: supply troops to fight fellow Southerners or join the Confederacy themselves. All four chose secession within the following weeks, roughly doubling the Confederacy's population and territory and setting the final geographic lines of the war that Fort Sumter had just begun.
